name: Erik Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half five, and out with Gareth by six. Highfold is a hill farm, six hundred ewes on the top ground and forty suckler cows lower down, with hay and a bit of barley in the valley. I'm usually on the quad checking the ewes, or fixing whatever's broken, because I was a mechanic for thirty years before this.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to Highfold?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The garage I worked at in the village closed when old Pritchard retired. It's a car wash now. Margit's family has farmed Highfold for three generations, and her brother Gareth said there's always work for family. So at fifty-four I started learning sheep, which is humbling, I'll tell you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet, and I like fixing things, the old baler, the quad, the water pumps. What's hard is the dogs. Gareth's dog, Fly, does what he says with one whistle. Mine looks at me like I'm a fool. Gareth says it's because I am, when it comes to sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always knew it was a lot of noise. I'd say it after chapel to the other farmers, and at the mart on a Tuesday. I don't go online, so they'd hear it from me in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news. Gareth's not going to buy anything clever anyway, and I'm not going to learn it. We'd carry on as we are, which is how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. Fix the baler before next summer, help with the tupping, keep saving a little each month, around a hundred and fifty. I'd maybe finally get my dog trained, if Gareth's patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the end of a long wet week when the sun comes out on the Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gareth's not going to buy anything clever anyway. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Hill farming doesn't pay enough to buy fancy machines. And he doesn't trust them. Neither do I. Every new tractor I worked on at the garage had more computer in it and less you could fix with a spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still bother you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. Lamb prices, feed prices, the bank. That's what decides if Highfold survives. Computers never came into it.

S0.say: I'd say I always knew it was a lot of noise. He'd say it after chapel and at the Tuesday mart, in person, never online.
S0.think: Privately it's good news: Gareth won't buy anything clever and Erik won't learn it, so they carry on as they should.
S0.do: Carries on at Highfold, fixes the baler before summer, helps with tupping and saves about 150 a month. Works on training his dog.
S0.feel: Calm, like sunshine on a Sunday after a long wet week.
S0.quote: Every new tractor I worked on at the garage had more computer in it and less you could fix with a spanner.
S0.fieldNote: Erik's distrust of technology comes from the workshop: machines he couldn't fix with a spanner. He sees farm survival entirely in terms of prices and the bank. His self-mockery about the dog shows warmth and humility about being junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have managed change before and we'll manage this. I'd also say the people in the cities making these things should come and try a hill in February. I'd say it at the mart, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the hill's safer than most places. Robots on flat fields, fine, but up on our top ground? It's rock and bog and fog. But the big lowland farms would get cheaper, and if their lamb's cheaper than ours, that's where it would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and see what happens. I wouldn't learn any of it unless Gareth asked me to, and he won't. I'd keep saving the same, and keep my head down and my tools sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, in the background. Like hearing a lorry on the lane at night and wondering where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some would say a mechanic is just the person to look after the new machines. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margit said the same. But I was a mechanic for engines, not computers. These new things, you plug a laptop in and it tells you what's wrong, and then you order a part from abroad. That's not mechanics, that's ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly for farms like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies and the government that lets them. Not the farmers. Farmers do what they have to. The people who'll make money from this never got their boots dirty.

S1.say: I'd say farmers have managed change before and will manage this, and the city people making the machines should try a hill in February.
S1.think: He thinks the hill is safer than most places because of rock, bog and fog, but cheaper lamb from robot-run lowland farms could still hurt Highfold.
S1.do: Keeps going and waits to see what happens, without learning the new tools unless Gareth asks. Keeps saving the same and keeps his tools sharp.
S1.feel: Uneasy in the background, like a lorry on the lane at night.
S1.fieldNote: Erik's resistance is rooted in pride in his trade; he doesn't see modern diagnostics as real mechanics. He sees the threat to the farm through prices, not through a robot replacing him. His blame falls on tech firms and government, never farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let this happen so fast, and the government should never have allowed it. I'd say it at the mart, at chapel, to anyone. But I'd also say that families like ours will look after each other, like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried for Highfold, more than for my job. Gareth would never let me go, I'm family. But if robot farms down the valley can sell lamb for half what ours costs, the farm itself goes under, and then there's no job for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away. We'd sell the second car, and Margit and I would stop the little trips to the coast. I'd talk to Gareth about what the farm can do, maybe more direct selling of our lamb to people who want it from a real hill. And I'd lean on the chapel and the family, because that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it, and I'd still sleep, mostly. But it'd be on my mind every time I looked at the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the family would look after each other. What would that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margit's sister has a café in town, and she'd sell our lamb there. My son Owen's a plumber, and if I had to, I'd go and carry pipes for him. I wouldn't take money from the government if family could help. That's how I was brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning let you do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Pay off the little we owe on the quad, maybe. Two years is one tupping and one lambing on a hill. You can't change a hill farm in two years.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness to allow this so fast and the government should never have let it happen, but families like ours will look after each other as always.
S2.think: He worries more for Highfold than for his job: Gareth would keep him as family, but cheap robot-farmed lamb could sink the whole farm.
S2.do: Sells the second car and stops trips to the coast straight away, and pays off the quad. Talks to Gareth about selling lamb directly, through Margit's sister's café, and would carry pipes for his son Owen rather than take government money.
S2.feel: Anxious and praying about it, but mostly still sleeping.
S2.quote: Two years is one tupping and one lambing on a hill. You can't change a hill farm in two years.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's faith and family ties soften what could be a harsher reaction; he feels protected by kinship, not savings. His fear is for the farm as a whole. Refusing government money in favour of family help is a firm point of principle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, so let's prepare, and not wait for the government to do it for us. I'd say it to the young farmers' club and at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three, and Highfold could change slowly in that time. I think the hill's safe for longer than the flat ground. My worry is still the price of lamb, not robots on our top field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and save a bit more, two hundred a month. I'd help Gareth set up selling our lamb straight to people, boxes for the freezer, through the café and the chapel. And I'd vote for whoever promised to keep family farms on their land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More time means we can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If they come, Gareth's son Dylan can learn them. He's twenty-three and he loves gadgets. I'll do the fixing on the old things for as long as there are old things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't wait for the government. Would you take help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was help to keep working, like a grant to share a machine between farms in the valley, I'd take it. If it was money for doing nothing, no. A man needs work.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, so let's prepare ourselves and not wait for the government to do it for us.
S3.think: At 63 he thinks the hill stays safe longer than flat ground, and the real worry remains lamb prices, not robots on the top field.
S3.do: Keeps going and saves about 200 a month, helps Gareth sell lamb freezer boxes directly through the café and chapel. Votes for whoever promises to keep family farms on their land.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with more time meaning they can do something.
S3.quote: If it was money for doing nothing, no. A man needs work.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Erik think about selling lamb directly, which fits his trust in community. He hands learning the machines to his nephew Dylan. He accepts help that keeps people working, a clear line in his values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who complains after that should have used the time. I'd say it at chapel and the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight and probably retired, or mostly. So it's not about me. It's about Dylan, and whether Highfold is still there for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd help Dylan get proper training, an apprenticeship maybe, in the new machines, because he's the future of the farm. I'd keep saving and fixing what I can. And I'd make sure Margit and I have the house sorted for when we stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but for the farm, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dylan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn it all, and to remember the hill. My father-in-law ran this hill with two dogs and a stick. If a robot can do it better, I'd like to see it find a ewe in a snowdrift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be sorry not to see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've been through enough change. The garage went, my old trade went, and I learned sheep at fifty-four. That's enough learning for one life.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who complains after that should have used the time. He'd say it at chapel and the mart.
S4.think: At 68 he'd be mostly retired, so it's not about him; it's about his nephew Dylan and whether Highfold is still there for him.
S4.do: Keeps working and helps Dylan get an apprenticeship in the new machines. Keeps saving and sorts out the house with Margit for retirement.
S4.feel: Uneasy, for the farm rather than himself.
S4.quote: The garage went, my old trade went, and I learned sheep at fifty-four. That's enough learning for one life.
S4.fieldNote: Erik's worry in the long picture is about the farm passing on, not about himself. He endorses apprenticeships for the young while refusing more learning for himself. The snowdrift line captures his doubt that machines can match the hill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Cheap robot lamb from the lowlands could sink Highfold before we'd even turned round. What would help is fair prices for family farms and help to share machines through the valley farmers' group, not handouts. And the family and the chapel standing together, like always.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about faith. People think it's old-fashioned. But when the garage closed, it was the chapel that brought food round while I found my feet. Whatever comes, that's what I'd trust.

headlineQuote: My father-in-law ran this hill with two dogs and a stick. If a robot can do it better, I'd like to see it find a ewe in a snowdrift.
portrait: Erik Abbott is 58, a former village mechanic who has spent four years as the junior hand at Highfold, his wife Margit's family hill farm, run by her brother Gareth. He's still learning the sheep and the dogs, has never used an AI tool and doesn't intend to, and his faith, his chapel and his family are where he looks for help, not the government. He blames tech companies and city decision-makers who've never worked land, and he trusts family loyalty to keep him on. He stays calm with a plateau, uneasy with steady change, and anxious with AGI in two years, mainly because cheap robot-farmed lamb could sink the whole farm. With more warning he leans on family and thrift, and in the ten-year picture his concern moves to his nephew and the farm's future.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because cheap robot-farmed lamb from the big lowland farms could sink Highfold before the family had time to adjust, and he'd be 60 with a few months saved.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping family farms on their land, through fair prices and help to share machines through the valley farmers' group rather than handouts, and his family and chapel standing together.
